answers: One of the two Secret Service supervisors to lose their jobs so far over the Colombia sex scandal joked that he was checking out Sarah Palin as he guarded her during the 2008 campaign, the Washington Post finds. Senior agent David Chaney posted at least two pictures of himself with Palin on Facebook, one with the comment, "I was really checking her out, if you know what I mean." Chaney has been forced to resign, and another supervisor has been informed that he will be fired. In an interview with Fox News, Palin said the joke is on Chaney. "Well check this out, buddy—you're fired!" she said, calling the scandal "a symptom of government run amok," reports AP. "It's like, who's minding the store around here?" she added. "The president, for one, he better be wary, there, of when Secret Service is accompanying his family on vacation. They may be checking out the first lady instead of guarding her."

The U.S. Secret Service has faced significant scrutiny following a prostitution scandal involving several of its agents during a security detail for President Barack Obama in Cartagena, Colombia. The incident, which occurred ahead of the Summit of the Americas in April 2010, has led to the firing of multiple employees and raised concerns about the agency's internal culture and oversight.

At the center of the controversy is David Chaney, a senior supervisor in the Secret Service’s international programs division, who was forced to resign after making inappropriate comments on Facebook about his duties during the 2008 presidential campaign. Chaney posted photos of himself standing behind Sarah Palin, a former Republican vice presidential candidate, and joked that he was “checking her out.” The comments, which were made in 2009, resurfaced in the media after the scandal broke, prompting Palin to respond on Fox News, joking that Chaney should be fired.

Chaney was not the only agent involved in the scandal. Greg Stokes, another supervisor, was also implicated and is expected to be fired. Both men were part of a larger group of 11 Secret Service agents and 10 military personnel who allegedly participated in a night of heavy drinking, visits to a strip club, and payments to prostitutes. The incident came to light after a dispute over payment with a prostitute at the Hotel Caribe, which led to the involvement of hotel staff and Colombian authorities.

In response, the Secret Service has taken swift action, firing three employees and placing others on administrative leave. Their top-secret security clearances have been revoked, and the agency has replaced the original security team with a new one. The Secret Service has also launched an internal investigation, with additional support from military personnel and Colombian authorities.

Lawmakers, including Rep. Peter King and Sen. Chuck Grassley, have expressed concerns about the scandal and expect more firings in the coming days. They have called for greater accountability and transparency within the agency. Meanwhile, President Obama’s chief spokesman, Jay Carney, has emphasized the need for patience as the investigation continues, stating that the president’s security was not compromised.

The scandal has sparked political debate, with some lawmakers suggesting that it reflects poor management under the Obama administration. Sarah Palin, in particular, has criticized the incident as a symptom of government dysfunction and called for greater oversight. However, the Secret Service has maintained that the incident was an isolated case and not indicative of a broader cultural issue within the agency.
